## What is a simulation?

**Experimentation with the help of a model.**

Choose a model, choose parameters, generate data, see what happens.

. . .

You already have both pieces:

- **Chapter 3:** a function for the expected value
- **Chapter 4:** a distribution for the noise around it

::: {.notes}
Worth saying plainly that nothing new is being introduced today, only combined.
They wrote Ricker and Michaelis-Menten functions in chapter 3 and met rnorm,
rbinom and rnbinom in chapter 4.

The one new idea is direction. Until now data came first and the model was
fitted to it. Today the model comes first and the data come out of it.
:::

## Why simulate?

- **Study design.** How many samples do I need to detect this effect?
- **Model checking.** Does my model produce data that look like my data?
- **Method checking.** Does this analysis recover the answer I put in?
- **Theory.** What happens if I add this mechanism?

. . .

The second and third are why this is not optional: it is how you find out
whether your analysis works **before** you trust it.

::: {.notes}
Study design is Thursday's lecture, power analysis, and part 3 of the midterm.

Method checking is the one worth dwelling on. If you simulate data with a known
slope of 1.5 and your analysis says 0.4, the analysis is wrong, and you found
out without needing a single real measurement. Real data cannot do that for you,
because you never know the true answer.

Bolker's framing in 5.1: simulation is how you make sure the pieces work
together before you commit to them.
:::

## The recipe

1. Pick a model, the deterministic part
2. Pick parameters
3. Add noise from a distribution
4. Look at the output
5. Change something and repeat

::: {.notes}
Five steps, and the rest of the lecture is three passes through them with
different pieces swapped in: a line with normal noise, a curve with negative
binomial noise, then groups.

Step 5 is where the learning happens, and it is also the step students skip.
:::

## Start with the deterministic part {.smaller}

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| fig-height: 2.4
a <- 2
b <- 1
x <- 1:20

y_det <- a + b * x

plot(x = x, y = y_det)
```
:::

A line: $y = a + bx$. No randomness yet.

::: {.notes}
Deliberately the simplest possible model, so the attention is on the structure
rather than on the function.

Note that y_det is a vector of 20 expected values, one per x. The noise gets
added to each of them in a moment.
:::

## Now add noise

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| fig-height: 2.8
y_stoch <- rnorm(n = 20, mean = y_det, sd = 2)

plot(x = x, y = y_stoch)
```
:::

`mean = y_det` is the trick: **a different mean for every point.**

::: {.notes}
This is the step that makes it a statistical model, and the vectorized mean is
the part worth pointing at. rnorm is given 20 means and returns 20 draws, one
around each.

Say it as a sentence: each observation is its expected value plus noise. That
sentence is every model in the rest of the course.
:::

## Run it again

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
y_stoch <- rnorm(n = 20, mean = y_det, sd = 2)
plot(x = x, y = y_stoch)
```
:::

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 3.2
par(mfrow = c(1, 4), mar = c(3.2, 3.2, 1.6, 0.6), mgp = c(1.9, 0.6, 0))
for (i in 1:4) {
  ys <- rnorm(n = 20, mean = y_det, sd = 2)
  plot(x, ys, pch = 16, col = "grey30", ylim = c(0, 28),
       xlab = "x", ylab = "y", main = paste("run", i))
  abline(a = 2, b = 1, col = "red", lwd = 2)
}
```

Same model, same parameters, four different datasets.

::: {.notes}
Have them run it several times themselves before showing this.

The point is the one students find genuinely surprising: the data are not the
model. Each dataset is one draw from a process, and the red line, the truth, is
the same in all four panels.

This is also the honest version of "my result did not replicate". Some of that
spread is just this.
:::

## When the noise grows with the mean {.smaller}

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| fig-height: 3.3
#| fig-width: 6
sd_multiplier <- 0.3

y_stoch <- rnorm(n = 20, mean = y_det, sd = y_det * sd_multiplier)

plot(x = x, y = y_stoch)
points(x, y_det, col = "blue")
```
:::

Bigger things vary more. Very common in biology.

::: {.notes}
Body size, abundance, biomass: in all of them the spread grows with the mean,
which is why a constant sd is often wrong.

Connect to Lecture 12: this is the multiplicative idea again. Constant
proportional variation is what makes data lognormal.

The blue points are the deterministic expectation, so the fan shape is visible
against it.
:::

## Your turn: break it {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
a <- 2
b <- 1
x <- 1:20
y_det <- a + b * x

y_stoch <- rnorm(n = 20, mean = y_det, sd = 2)
plot(x = x, y = y_stoch)
abline(a = a, b = b, col = "red")

# now try
# sd = 0.1    sd = 20    b = 0    b = -1
```
:::

How big does `sd` have to be before the line is invisible in the data?

::: {.notes}
Six minutes. The last question has no single right answer and that is the point:
whether a pattern is visible depends on the ratio of signal to noise, not on
either one alone.

With sd = 20 and this slope, the line is hopeless with 20 points. That is
exactly the question power analysis answers on Thursday, so this exercise is the
setup for it.

b = 0 is worth doing too: it shows what "no effect" data look like, which is the
thing they will be testing against all semester.
:::

## A curve instead of a line

Bolker's example: a hyperbolic function with **negative binomial** noise.

$$y = \frac{a\,b}{b + x}$$

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 2.6
par(mar = c(3.4, 3.4, 0.6, 0.6), mgp = c(2, 0.6, 0))
a2 <- 20; b2 <- 1
xx <- runif(50, min = 0, max = 5)
plot(xx, a2 * b2 / (b2 + xx), pch = 16, col = "grey30",
     xlab = "x", ylab = "expected y")
```

Why would a normal error term be wrong here?

::: {.notes}
Section 5.2 in the book. Two things are new: the deterministic part is a curve,
and the noise is a count distribution.

Answer to the question on the slide: y is a count, so it cannot be negative and
it cannot be fractional, and near the right side the expected value is small
enough that a normal would predict negative counts. Counts need a count
distribution.

Note runif for the x values: the predictor itself is random here, which is what
an observational study looks like. Worth asking how that differs from x <- 0:5,
which is a designed experiment with fixed levels.
:::

## Adding negative binomial noise {.smaller}

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| fig-height: 3.2
#| fig-width: 6
a <- 20
b <- 1
k <- 5
x <- runif(50, min = 0, max = 5)

y_det <- a * b / (b + x)
y <- rnbinom(n = 50, mu = y_det, size = k)

plot(x = x, y = y)
```
:::

::: {.notes}
Run it several times. The scatter is wider at the left, where the mean is
larger, which is what a negative binomial does automatically: its variance grows
with its mean.

k is the clumping parameter of the negative binomial from the bestiary in
Lecture 12. Small k, more scatter. They estimate one from real data later
today.

Note the model written correctly as a * b / (b + x). With b = 1 that is the same
as a / (b + x), which is why the old version of this slide looked fine, but the
two differ as soon as b is not 1, which happens on the group slides shortly.
:::

## Your turn: what does each parameter do? {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
a <- 20
b <- 1
k <- 5
x <- runif(50, min = 0, max = 5)

y_det <- a * b / (b + x)
y <- rnbinom(n = 50, mu = y_det, size = k)

plot(x = x, y = y, ylim = c(0, 60))
points(x, y_det, col = "blue", pch = 16)
```
:::

Try `k = 0.5` and `k = 100`. Then `a = 50`. Then `b = 3`.

::: {.notes}
Seven minutes.

What to listen for: a sets the starting height, b controls how fast the curve
drops, and k controls only the scatter, not the expectation. That last one is
the distinction that matters: a and b are the biology, k is the noise.

k = 100 looks almost Poisson, k = 0.5 is wild. Same expected curve underneath
both, which is the blue points.
:::

## Groups {.center}

## Different species, different parameters

Two species, 25 observations each. They differ in `a` and `b`, but share the
same noise.

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
g <- factor(rep(1:2, each = 25))

a <- c(20, 10)
b <- c(1, 2)
```
:::

`a` and `b` are now **vectors**, one value per group.

::: {.notes}
Groups are the first structural idea of the course: until now every
observation came from one process, and here there are two. Building it is the
easiest way to see it, and it is also how a real dataset with two species, two
sites or two sexes is put together.

factor() matters: g is a grouping label, not the number 1 or 2. R will use it to
pick parameters and to pick colors.
:::

## Indexing by group {.smaller}

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| fig-height: 2.2
x <- runif(50, min = 0, max = 5)

y_det <- a[g] * b[g] / (b[g] + x)

plot(x = x, y = y_det, col = g, pch = 16)
```
:::

`a[g]` reads "the `a` for whichever group this observation belongs to".

::: {.notes}
a[g] is the piece of R syntax worth slowing down on. g is a factor of 1s and 2s,
so a[g] is a 50-long vector made of a[1] and a[2] in the right places.

Have them try a[1] and a[2] on their own to see the pieces.

col = g colors the points by group, because R converts the factor to 1 and 2 and
those are the first two colors in the palette. pch = g works the same way for
symbols.
:::

## Now add the noise

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| fig-height: 2.8
k <- 5

y <- rnbinom(n = 50, mu = y_det, size = k)

plot(x = x, y = y, col = g, pch = as.numeric(g))
legend("topright", bty = "n", col = 1:2, pch = 1:2,
       legend = c("species 1", "species 2"))
```
:::

::: {.notes}
Plotting it badly first is worth doing: without col and pch the two species are
indistinguishable, which is the honest version of the question "could I even
tell these apart in real data?".

The legend is the Lecture 8 habit arriving in base graphics.

Ask the room: do the two species look different here? With k = 5 and this much
overlap it is genuinely arguable, which leads into the next slide.
:::

## Your turn: can you tell them apart? {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
a <- c(20, 10)      # change these
b <- c(1, 2)
k <- 5

y_det <- a[g] * b[g] / (b[g] + x)
y <- rnbinom(n = 50, mu = y_det, size = k)
plot(x = x, y = y, col = g, pch = as.numeric(g))
```
:::

Find parameters where the two species look **clearly different**.
Then find parameters where they look **identical**.
Then find parameters where they differ only at **low x**.

::: {.notes}
Eight minutes, and the best exercise in the lecture. It is a real research
question in disguise: how different do two groups have to be before you could
detect it with 25 observations each?

The third case, differing only at low x, is the interesting one. It is common in
real data and it is why where you sample matters as much as how much you sample.
Anyone who finds it has learned something about study design that no amount of
reading would teach.

Raising k makes everything easier to see, which is the same lesson as the sd
exercise earlier.
:::

## Choosing the pieces {.center}

## Three choices, every time

A simulation needs all three before it will run:

1. **The model.** What shape does the average follow?
2. **The distribution.** How do observations scatter around it?
3. **The parameters.** What numbers go in?

. . .

You have done the first two already, on real data. Today they get used in the
other direction.

::: {.notes}
Worth naming as a checklist, because a simulation will not run until all three
are chosen. Vagueness you can get away with when describing data becomes
impossible when you have to generate it.

That is the hidden benefit of simulating: it catches the places where you have
not actually decided anything.

One slide each, next.
:::

## 1. The model: what shape? {.smaller}

From chapter 3, Lectures 9 and 10. Ask three questions of the pattern:

- What happens at the **left end**?
- What happens at the **right end**?
- What happens **in between**: rise, fall, peak, level off, switch?

. . .

| Shape | Function |
|---|---|
| Straight | $a + bx$ |
| Rises and levels off | Michaelis-Menten, Holling type II |
| Humped | Ricker, power-Ricker |
| Falling | negative exponential |
| Flat then a switch | hockey stick, threshold |

::: {.notes}
Deliberately the same three questions as the bestiary slide in Lecture 10, and
the same table in miniature.

Two routes to a choice, both legitimate: the shape the data have, which is the
phenomenological route, or the mechanism you believe, which is the mechanistic
one. The tadpole functional response was both.

If there is no predictor, the answer to "what shape" is a flat line: the
expected value is the same for every observation. That is a perfectly good
model, and two of the three worked examples later are exactly that case.

For a simulation there is a third route, which is what you want to test. If the
question is "could I detect a hump", simulate a hump.
:::

## 2. The distribution: what kind of number? {.smaller}

From chapter 4, Lecture 12. Eliminate, then check:

- **Discrete or continuous?**
- **What range?** 0 to 1, 0 upward, any number
- **What process made it?** Out of a known total, a count with no ceiling,
  a measurement, a waiting time

. . .

Then **use a number, not an impression**:

- Counts: is the variance bigger than the mean? Poisson or negative binomial
- Continuous and positive: is the mean far from the median? Lognormal or gamma

::: {.notes}
The elimination steps are from the "how do you choose" slide in Lecture 12, and
the two checks are the ones they will use on the midterm.

In R this is the choice between rnorm, rbinom, rpois, rnbinom, rlnorm and so on.
The r functions are the simulation half of the four-letter family.

Say the pairing out loud: the model sets the mean, the distribution sets the
scatter around it. On the slides so far that is `mean = y_det` inside rnorm, and
`mu = y_det` inside rnbinom.
:::

## 3. The parameters: where do the numbers come from? {.smaller}

You have to put numbers in. Four honest sources:

1. **Pilot data.** Even 10 observations give you a rough mean and spread.
2. **Published studies** on the same system, or a similar one. Methods sections
   and figures have numbers in them.
3. **Your own previous data.** The variance from last season is usually the best
   guess for next season.
4. **Biological limits.** A proportion is between 0 and 1, a clutch is not 400
   eggs, a seedling does not weigh a kilogram.

. . .

And when you genuinely do not know: **try a range** and see whether the answer
changes.

::: {.notes}
This is the question students ask as soon as they try it on their own system,
and it has a reputation for being a dark art. It is not.

Source 1 is the most useful and the most ignored. A single afternoon of pilot
sampling turns a guess into an estimate, and it also finds the problems with your
protocol while they are cheap to fix.

The fallback matters just as much: if you cannot pin down a number, run the
simulation across a plausible range of it. If the conclusion holds across the
range, the uncertainty did not matter. If it flips, you have learned that this
number is worth measuring before you commit.

Spreading one parameter across a range and watching the answer move is exactly
what Thursday does with sample size and noise.
:::

## The one number nobody can give you

**How big an effect would matter?**

A 2% change in growth rate might be real and still not be worth designing a
study around.

. . .

Simulate the **smallest effect you would care about**, not the biggest one you
hope for.

::: {.notes}
The one parameter no dataset can give them, because it is a judgment about the
biology, not a measurement.

Why it matters practically: a study powered for a huge effect will miss the
modest one you are likely to have, and designing around your most optimistic
guess is the most common way power analyses mislead people.

Ask the room for their own systems. If their study found a difference of X,
would anyone change what they do? That number is the one to simulate.

Thursday's lecture is built on this: power only means anything once you have
said how big an effect you want to be able to detect.
:::

## Three worked examples, on real data {.center}

## Example 1: the tadpoles, again

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 3.2
par(mar = c(3.4, 3.4, 0.6, 0.6), mgp = c(2, 0.6, 0))
plot(frogs$Initial, frogs$Killed, pch = 16, cex = 1.5, col = "black",
     xlab = "tadpoles in the tank", ylab = "number killed",
     xlim = c(0, 100), ylim = c(0, 40))
curve(60 * x / (100 + x), add = TRUE, col = "red", lwd = 2)
```

Lecture 10 gave us the curve. Each tank started with a known number, so the
kills are **out of** that number: binomial.

::: {.notes}
Same dataset they fitted by eye in Lecture 10, with a = 60 and b = 100 for the
Michaelis-Menten curve.

The binomial part may need a sentence: the response is a number killed out of a
known starting number, which is the "out of" phrasing from the bestiary. That is
all it takes to pick the distribution here.

Today those two halves become a generator: a curve for the expected number
killed, and binomial noise around it.
:::

## Simulate the experiment {.smaller}

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| fig-height: 2.2
p <- (60 * frogs$Initial / (100 + frogs$Initial)) / frogs$Initial

killed_sim <- rbinom(n = nrow(frogs), size = frogs$Initial, prob = p)

plot(frogs$Initial, killed_sim, pch = 16, col = "red",
     xlab = "tadpoles in the tank", ylab = "number killed")
points(frogs$Initial, frogs$Killed, pch = 1, cex = 1.4)
```
:::

Red: a fake experiment. Open circles: the real one.

::: {.notes}
This is the most important idea in the lecture: if your model is any good, data
simulated from it should be hard to tell from the real thing.

Walk the first line slowly. The curve gives the expected number killed; dividing
by Initial turns that into a per-tadpole probability, which is what rbinom wants.

Run it several times. Sometimes the fake data look like the real data,
sometimes they do not, and the honest conclusion with 16 points is that this
model is not obviously wrong, which is as much as these data support.

In chapter 6 this becomes a formal check. Here it is eyeball.
:::

## Example 2: counting cardinals

Breeding Bird Survey, Florida, 2019. One count per route, 71 routes.

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="68%"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 2.8
#| fig-width: 6.3
hist(cardinals, breaks = seq(0, 180, by = 10), col = "grey85",
     main = "", xlab = "cardinals counted on a route")
```
:::

::: {.column width="30%"}
![](figures/northern_cardinal.jpg)

[*Cardinalis cardinalis*]{style="font-size:0.7em"}<br>
[Photo: USFWS, public domain]{style="font-size:0.45em; color:#777"}
:::

::::

A count with no ceiling. **Poisson?**

::: {.notes}
Real data from the course repository, `data/BBS/`, and a dataset some of them may
use for the midterm.

One row per route: a volunteer stops every half mile along a 24.5 mile route and
counts every bird heard or seen.

Run the shape test from the bestiary: counts, no fixed ceiling, so Poisson is the
first guess. The next slide checks that rather than taking it on faith.
:::

## A Poisson makes a testable claim

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
mean(cardinals)
var(cardinals)
var(cardinals) / mean(cardinals)
```
:::

A Poisson has **mean = variance**, so that ratio should be about 1.

It is **28**: far more spread than a Poisson allows.

::: {.notes}
Two lines of code, and it works on any count data they will ever have. Around 1
means a Poisson is plausible; much more than 1 means overdispersion, which is
what real ecological counts almost always look like.

Why cardinals clump: habitat varies between routes, some suburban, some pine
flatwoods, and birds respond to that. Variation in the rate between routes is
exactly the negative binomial story from the bestiary.

This is new to them. The bestiary slide said the negative binomial is for clumped
counts; this is how you find out whether yours are.
:::

## Matching a negative binomial, then simulating from it

The negative binomial has a mean and a clumping parameter. Solve for both from
the data, then generate fake routes:

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
mu <- mean(cardinals)
size <- mu^2 / (var(cardinals) - mu)      # about 1.8

fake <- rnbinom(n = 71, mu = mu, size = size)

hist(fake)
hist(cardinals)
```
:::

::: {.notes}
The `size` line is the method of moments: set the distribution's mean and
variance equal to the data's, then solve. It is the simplest way to fit a
distribution and it needs no optimizer. Chapter 6 replaces it with maximum
likelihood.

size = 1.8 is heavy clumping. Above about 10 it would look nearly Poisson.

Then the point of today: having fitted it, run it forwards. Have them do that
several times before the next slide, holding one question in mind, which is
whether they could tell a fake set of 71 routes from the real set.
:::

## Fake routes against real ones

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 3.4
#| fig-width: 9
mu <- mean(cardinals); sz <- mu^2 / (var(cardinals) - mu)
par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(3.4, 3.4, 2.2, 0.6), mgp = c(2, 0.6, 0))
brks <- seq(0, 260, by = 20)
hist(cardinals, breaks = brks, col = "grey70", main = "real", xlab = "count")
for (i in 1:2) {
  hist(rnbinom(71, mu = mu, size = sz), breaks = brks, col = "lightsteelblue",
       main = paste("simulated", i), xlab = "count")
}
```

Close enough that you could not pick the real one out of a line-up.

. . .

A Poisson would never do this: it cannot make a 175.

::: {.notes}
This is the model check, done honestly. The simulated sets have the same kind of
long right tail and the same pile of low counts.

Worth running it live a few times, because occasionally a simulated set looks
wrong, and that is useful too: one dataset is one draw.

If someone asks what would count as a failure: simulated data that never reach
the real maximum, or that are symmetric when the real data are skewed. That is
exactly what a Poisson gives here.
:::

## Example 3: how much data do you need to see a shape?

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 3.4
#| fig-width: 9
lm_mass <- mean(log10(avonet$Mass)); ls_mass <- sd(log10(avonet$Mass))
par(mfrow = c(1, 4), mar = c(3.2, 3.2, 2.2, 0.6), mgp = c(1.9, 0.6, 0))
for (n in c(10, 50, 200, 5000)) {
  draws <- rlnorm(n, meanlog = lm_mass * log(10), sdlog = ls_mass * log(10))
  hist(log10(draws), breaks = 15, col = "grey85", main = paste("n =", n),
       xlab = "log10 mass")
}
```

All four are lognormal, with the parameters of real bird masses.

::: {.notes}
The point of the lecture, applied to their own assignment: with 10 observations
you cannot see a distribution's shape, and with 50 you can barely argue about
it.

Use this when a student says their Assignment 2 variable "does not look like
anything". If they have 30 points, that may be all it means.

The parameters come from AVONET body mass, converted to natural log for rlnorm,
so these are plausible bird faunas rather than invented numbers.
:::

## Your turn: how few is too few? {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
draws <- rlnorm(n = 20, meanlog = 3.5, sdlog = 1.6)

hist(log10(draws), breaks = 15)

# run it several times at n = 20, then try n = 100, n = 1000
```
:::

At what sample size does the shape stop changing every time you run it?

::: {.notes}
Six minutes, and the most directly useful exercise for the midterm and the
final.

There is no single answer, which is the lesson. For a roughly symmetric
distribution a few dozen points is often enough; for a skewed one with a long
tail you need hundreds before the histogram settles down.

The habit worth naming: when you are not sure whether a feature in your data is
real, simulate data without it and see how often the feature shows up anyway.
:::

## You do not always need a curve {.smaller}

| Example | Deterministic part | Distribution |
|---|---|---|
| Tadpoles | Michaelis-Menten curve | binomial |
| Cardinals | just a mean | negative binomial |
| Bird masses | just a mean | lognormal |

. . .

A curve is only needed when the expected value **changes with a predictor**.
With one variable and no predictor, the distribution is the whole model.

::: {.notes}
Worth being explicit, because the recipe slide said "a curve plus a
distribution" and two of the three examples had no curve in them.

The tadpoles had a predictor, the number of tadpoles in the tank, so the
expected number killed changes along it. Cardinals and bird masses are single
variables: the expected value is the same for every observation, so the
deterministic part is just a constant.

Both are models. One is `rbinom(n, size, prob = curve(x))`, the other is
`rnbinom(n, mu = a number, size)`.

Where this comes back: in chapter 6 the constant becomes a parameter to
estimate, and the two cases stop looking different at all.
:::

## What the three examples had in common

1. **Build the data your model predicts.**
2. **Compare it to what you actually got.**
3. **Repeat it**, because one dataset is one draw.

. . .

That is model checking, and it is most of what simulation is for.

::: {.notes}
Tadpoles, cardinals, bird masses: a binomial, a negative binomial and a
lognormal, each checked against real data from the course repository.

Step 3 is the one people skip, and it is the one that separates "my model looks
fine" from knowing how much variation to expect.

Thursday turns the same machinery into a number: how often would a study like
mine detect an effect that is really there?
:::

## What simulation buys you: 10 sites or 40? {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 4.1
#| fig-width: 7
run_study <- function(n) {
  x <- sample(1:20, n, replace = TRUE)
  y <- rnorm(n, mean = 2 + 1 * x, sd = 8)
  summary(lm(y ~ x))$coefficients["x", c("Estimate", "Pr(>|t|)")]
}
par(mfrow = c(2, 1), mar = c(3.4, 3.4, 2.0, 0.6), mgp = c(2, 0.6, 0))
for (n in c(10, 40)) {
  res <- t(replicate(1000, run_study(n)))
  detected <- mean(res[, 2] < 0.05)
  hist(res[, 1], breaks = seq(-2.5, 4.5, by = 0.1), col = "grey85",
       xlim = c(-1.5, 3.5), xlab = "estimated slope",
       main = sprintf("n = %d:  detected the effect %.0f%% of the time",
                      n, 100 * detected))
  abline(v = 1, col = "red", lwd = 3)
}
```

Same truth, same noise. **1000 studies each.**

::: {.notes}
The true slope is 1, the red line, and every one of these 2000 studies was done
honestly.

With 10 sites the estimates run from about -0.6 to 2.9, and a few come out
negative, pointing the wrong way entirely. With 40 they run from about 0.3 to
1.7.

The percentages are the decision-relevant part. Running the small study means
missing a real effect more than half the time, which is a lot of field work for
a coin flip. The large one essentially always finds it.

Say the name now: that percentage is **power**, and computing it is exactly
Thursday's lecture and Part 3 of the midterm. The only new thing on Thursday is
sweeping it across many parameter values instead of two.

This is also the honest answer to "why does my result disagree with the
published one". Two studies, same truth, different draws. Nobody did anything
wrong.

Callback worth making: they saw a figure like the top panel in Lecture 3 as a
finished picture. Now they can build it.
:::

## Start simple

- Simple models are easier to check and debug
- Complexity adds realism, and new ways to be wrong
- Add one piece at a time, and look after each one

Section **5.2.2.2** has a more complex worked example.

::: {.notes}
The advice is Bolker's and it is the same advice as writing functions in chapter
3: build a small piece, check it, then extend.

Practical version for the midterm: get a line with noise working before adding
groups.
:::
